title.en: Kaguya-hime: The Shining Princess Returns to the Moon

region.en: A bamboo grove outside the Heian capital; the moon capital above (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 京城郊外竹林；天上月之都（象徵定位）

texts.period: Taketori Monogatari composed c. late 9th–early 10th century CE (oldest surviving tale in Japanese; trans. Dickins 1888)

source.archive: Internet Archive / Project Gutenberg (Dickins 1888 translation; Davis 1912 retelling)
source.work: Taketori Monogatari (The Tale of the Bamboo-Cutter), trans. Frederick Victor Dickins, 1888; retold in F. Hadland Davis, Myths & Legends of Japan (1912)

summary.en: A childless bamboo-cutter finds a four-inch girl shining inside a bamboo stalk; in three months she grows into the peerless Lady Kaguya, whose impossible quests defeat five noble suitors and even the emperor's love. As the full moon approaches she remembers she was sent from the moon capital; the Moonfolk descend, dress her in the robe that erases mortality, and ascend — leaving the elixir of life that the emperor burns on Japan's highest peak, giving Fuji its name, 'Never-Dying'.
summary.zh: 老翁於竹中拾得四寸輝夜姬；三月而成絕色，以難題卻五大臣，帝亦不得其身。望月之期將至，公主憶起月都之命；月人乘雲而降，為其著羽衣，塵心頓忘，乘雲昇天。所遺不死之藥，帝命焚於駿河最高之山，故富士山名曰「不死」。

sensitivity.note: Court tale (monogatari) of the Heian period drawing on moon-veneration imagery; passages are condensed paraphrases of public-domain translations (Dickins 1888; Davis 1912), presented for comparative mythology. The 'elixir gives Fuji its name' aetiology is read as folk etymology, not as an imperial claim.

passages.text: An old bamboo-cutter named Taketori no Okina went into the groves and cut reeds as he had always done, until one stalk glowed like sunlight and split open to reveal a girl four inches tall. He carried her home, and he and his wife reared her in a basket. Every time he cut cane thereafter, gold appeared among the stems, and in three months the child grew to a woman of peerless beauty, who was named Kaguya-hime, the Shining Princess. The old man's house filled with suitors, and their ranks swelled until five noblemen of the highest courts remained, vowing to win her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taketori Monogatari, opening (trans. Dickins 1888; cf. Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: Kaguya-hime demanded what could not be gotten: the stone begging-bowl of the Buddha of India; jeweled branches from the island of Hōrai; a robe of fire-rat fur that no flame can burn; a jewel from the dragon's neck that changes colour through five hues; and a cowry born from the swallow. Each suitor returned with a counterfeit, and she unmasked them one by one — the bowl proved common, the branch's jewels were paste, the fire-rat robe burned in the fire-test, the dragon jewel was bought from a conjurer's merchant, and the swallow's cowry was a bird's droppings. Word of her beauty reached the emperor himself, but the princess refused the palace; still he wrote to her, and she answered him in verses until his heart grew ever more tender.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taketori Monogatari, the five impossible quests episode (trans. Dickins 1888; cf. Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: As the autumn moon grew fuller, Kaguya-hime wept when she saw it, and at last confessed to the old couple: she was not of this world, but of the moon capital, whence she had been sent for a fault, and the day of her return was at hand. The emperor, told of this, sent two thousand soldiers to guard the house against the moon-people, yet when the moon rose, a shining cloud descended, and no bow-arm could draw against it. The messenger from the moon hung a robe of wings beside her; whoever wore it ceased to feel love or grief. She wrote her last verses to the emperor, prayed him never to send again for her, donned the robe so that her mortal thoughts fell away with her tears, and ascended with the cloud, leaving behind a vial of the elixir of immortality and a letter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taketori Monogatari, the moon-descension and ascent (trans. Dickins 1888; cf. Davis 1912); not verbatim.

passages.text: The emperor, seeing the elixir without the one being who could make life sweet, ordered it burned on the mountain nearest heaven, where the smoke rose highest; the mount of Suruga ever after bore the name Fuji, meaning 'Never-Dying', and smoke was said to rise from its summit to this day. The letters of the princess he kept, and his own men who had gazed upon the moon wept at the summit of that smoke.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Taketori Monogatari, the Fuji aetiology (trans. Dickins 1888; cf. Davis 1912); not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The Taketori Monogatari, commonly called the Tale of the Bamboo-Cutter, is the oldest surviving monogatari in Japanese literature, composed around the end of the ninth or the beginning of the tenth century CE. Though a courtly romance rather than a shrine myth, its matter is entirely mythic: a divine child from the moon who enters the human world by miraculous birth, blesses it with gold, defeats its most powerful men with impossible quests, and finally re-ascends, refusing the immortality of heaven to anyone who cannot share it with her. It is Japan's great otherworld-voyage tale told in reverse — the visitor is the otherworld, and the mortals are the ones who long to follow.

The tale opens on a poor bamboo-cutter, Taketori no Okina, who cuts cane for a living and has neither son nor daughter. One night a stalk shines at the base like sunlight, and inside he finds a girl four inches tall, of exquisite form. He carries her home to his wife, and the couple raise the child in a basket with tenderness. From that day every stalk he cuts bears gold, and the cutter grows rich in a few months. The child, meanwhile, grows from four inches to full stature in three months, more radiant than any woman in Japan, and is named Kaguya-hime. Word of her spreads; suitors fill the house night after night until only the most determined remain — five noblemen of the highest rank — and the old man, anxious for his foster-daughter, urges her to take a husband.

Kaguya-hime sets each suitor an impossible quest: the stone begging-bowl of the Buddha in India; jeweled branches from the immortal island of Hōrai; the fur robe of the fire-rat that no flame can burn; the jewel from the dragon-king's neck that shifts through five colours; and the cowry-shell that lies in the nest of the swallow. Each man returns with a treasure, and each treasure proves counterfeit: the bowl is common crockery, the jewels on the branch are paste that runs, the fur robe burns in the hearth, the dragon-jewel comes from a conjurer's merchant, and the cowry from the swallow is bird's dung. The suitors slink away in disgrace, and the tale lingers over their humiliation — the closest the monogatari comes to social satire, ridiculing wealth, rank and bravado before a girl who cannot be bought.

Last of all the emperor himself hears of the princess and visits; her radiance dazzles him, he begs her to come to the palace, and she refuses. Still he writes to her, and she answers in verse, and for three years they exchange poems while he does not press his claim further — an almost unprecedented gesture of restraint in a Heian tale of imperial desire.

But the princess has been looking at the moon with tears. As autumn's full moon draws near she confesses to the old couple that she is not of this world: she was sent down from the moon capital as punishment, and the time of her recall has come. The emperor, hearing of it, orders two thousand soldiers to encircle the house, yet when the moon rises a cloud of light descends, and against the moon-people no arrow will fly. The celestial messenger hangs a robe of wings beside her, and whoever wears it forgets all mortal grief. She writes her farewell to the emperor, praying him never to send for her again, for in heaven he cannot be followed; she sets down a letter and a vial of the elixir of immortality; she robes herself and her tears and her love fall away like a garment, and she ascends with the cloud into the moon.

The emperor, unable either to follow her or to make his court immortal without her, orders the elixir burned on the summit of the mountain in Suruga nearest to heaven. The smoke rises highest there, and the mountain takes the name Fuji, 'Never-Dying'; its summit is said to smoke to this day. The princess's letters he keeps with his own until his death. The tale thus closes its double aetiology — of Fuji's name and of the unbridgeable distance between men and gods — and the old cutter and his wife are left with the house their gold built and a daughter's empty room.
narrative._comment: narrative in prose; functions array separately

functions: Aetiology of Mount Fuji's name (fushi, 'never-dying') and of the elixir of immortality motif in Japanese narrative; the mountain is the smoke-channel between heaven and earth.
Charter for moon-veneration imagery in Japanese court poetry and the autumn full-moon festival (Jūgoya); the moon is a homeland, not a lamp.
Satire of Heian aristocratic courtship: the five suitors and their counterfeits ridicule status, wealth and bravado, making the tale a mirror of court society.
Refusal of imperial authority: even the emperor cannot bind the divine visitor, dramatising the gulf between human rule and heavenly beings.

variants.name: Taketori Monogatari (classical recension, c. 909 CE)
variants.text_tradition: Old Japanese monogatari; the oldest surviving manuscript recensions (Sanogi-bon, Hosomi-bon)
variants.summary: The full tale as outlined: miraculous bamboo birth, five quests, imperial courtship, moon-descension, elixir burned on Fuji.

variants.name: F. Hadland Davis retelling (1912)
variants.summary: Davis's condensed Edwardian retelling that popularised the tale in English; names the cutter Sanugi no Miyakko and stresses the Fuji aetiology.

variants.name: Princess Moonlight (Japanese Fairy Tale Series, No. 15, 1886)
variants.text_tradition: Kobunsha bilingual fairy-tale chapbook, trans. T. H. James (1886)
variants.summary: Meiji-era chapbook abridgement for children, emphasising the robe of wings and the ascent; circulated the tale internationally as a Japanese 'fairy tale'.
